title: State v. Pagliai
description: Whether parties in a criminal case can, by plea agreement, confer on the district court the authority to assess costs in dismissed cases, with the State arguing such agreements are permissible based on precedent, and the defendant arguing the court lacks statutory authority for such assessments.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that its precedents (State v. Petrie and State v. McMurry) allow parties to bargain for the assessment of costs in dismissed cases, and that Pagliai waived any challenge by entering the plea agreement.
defendant_argument: Pagliai argued that the district court lacked statutory authority to assess costs in dismissed cases, making the dispositional orders invalid, and that such an unauthorized disposition cannot be cured by contract, waiver, or estoppel.
decision_outcome: The court conditionally vacated the convictions, sentences, and dispositional orders, and remanded the case, allowing the State to either vacate only the cost assessment or vacate the entire plea bargain and reinstate all charges.

title: State Public Defender v. Iowa District Court for Scott County
description: Whether a district court has a role in determining if a local public defender is experiencing a temporary overload of cases, which would allow the public defender to return cases to the court.
plaintiff_argument: The State Public Defender argued that the local public defender has sole authority to determine if a temporary overload exists and can return cases to the court, which the court must accept.
defendant_argument: The Iowa District Court for Scott County, through the attorney general, argued that the court has a role in determining if a temporary overload exists and acted within its discretion to deny withdrawal motions, especially when no other attorneys were available.
decision_outcome: The court sustained the State Public Defender's writ of certiorari, vacating the district court's orders that denied the Davenport Public Defender's motions to withdraw from cases due to temporary overload.

title: State v. Hidlebaugh
description: Whether sentencing a defendant to prison based on their financial inability to purchase a home, as stipulated in a plea agreement, violates their constitutional rights to equal protection and due process, even if they made good faith efforts.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the district court's sentence was proper, based on the plea agreement and Hidlebaugh's criminal history, and that the Bearden v. Georgia precedent, concerning probation revocation, does not apply to initial sentencing decisions.
defendant_argument: Hidlebaugh argued that his imprisonment, resulting from his financial inability to purchase a home despite good faith efforts, violated his constitutional rights to equal protection and due process.
decision_outcome: The court vacated the Court of Appeals decision and Hidlebaugh's sentence, remanding the case for resentencing, stating that the district court may not consider the plea agreement's recommendation for prison based on Hidlebaugh's failure to buy a house unless it finds he did not use best efforts.

title: State v. Woods
description: Whether there is a federal or state constitutional right to carry a firearm while simultaneously in the illegal possession of a controlled substance or while committing an indictable offense.
plaintiff_argument: The State of Iowa argued that there is no federal or state constitutional right to carry a firearm while committing a crime, specifically while illegally possessing a controlled substance or committing an indictable offense.
defendant_argument: Kevin Dwayne Woods, Jr. argued that his conviction for carrying a dangerous weapon while illegally possessing a controlled substance violates his federal and state constitutional right to keep and bear arms.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed Kevin Woods's conviction for violating Iowa Code section 724.8B, ruling that there is no constitutional right to carry a firearm while committing a crime.

title: State v. Scullark
description: Whether the search of a defendant's fanny pack, which he attempted to pass to another person before being handcuffed, violated his constitutional rights against unreasonable searches and seizures under the United States and Iowa Constitutions.
plaintiff_argument: The search was a valid search incident to arrest because the fanny pack was immediately associated with Scullark's person at the time of arrest, making it subject to a categorical rule allowing full searches without additional justification.
defendant_argument: The search violated his constitutional rights because he was unable to access the fanny pack when it was searched, and the search did not serve the purposes of officer safety or evidence preservation, thus the "reaching-distance" rule should apply.
decision_outcome: The court vacated the court of appeals decision and affirmed the district court order denying Scullark's motion to suppress, thereby upholding the search of the fanny pack.

title: State v. Cole
description: Whether Jordan Kevin Cole's convictions for possessing firearms while under a domestic violence protective order violate his Second Amendment and Iowa Constitution Article I, Section 1A rights, or if he waived these rights by consenting to the order.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that Cole waived his constitutional rights to possess firearms by voluntarily consenting to the protective order, which explicitly prohibited him from possessing firearms.
defendant_argument: Cole argued that the firearm prohibition was unconstitutional and that he did not waive his Second Amendment and Iowa Constitution Article I, Section 1A rights, especially since the consent order lacked an express judicial finding of dangerousness.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed Cole's convictions for possessing firearms while under a domestic violence protective order but remanded the case for entry of a corrected sentencing order.

title: Sikora v. Iowa
description: Whether state officials are immune from state-law tort claims for money damages arising from wrongful imprisonment, or if such claims can proceed against individual state employees under common law or constitutional tort theories.
plaintiff_argument: Sikora argues that he was wrongfully imprisoned for nearly five months due to a miscalculation and that sovereign immunity should not bar his constitutional tort claims or common law claims for negligence, negligence per se, and false imprisonment against individual state employees.
defendant_argument: The State of Iowa and its director argue that sovereign immunity bars all of Sikora's state-law tort claims for money damages arising from wrongful imprisonment, and that the overruling of Godfrey v. State eliminated constitutional tort claims for damages.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the district court's dismissal of Sikora's suit, ruling that sovereign immunity bars his state-law money damages claims for wrongful imprisonment against the state and its employees.

title: State v. Amble
description: Whether Iowa Code section 808.16, which declares curbside garbage as abandoned property, is constitutional and allows for warrantless searches, with the State arguing it is constitutional and defendants arguing it is unconstitutional as a violation of privacy rights.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that Iowa Code section 808.16 is constitutional, making curbside garbage abandoned property and thus not protected by Article I, Section 8 of the Iowa Constitution, allowing warrantless searches.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that Iowa Code section 808.16 is facially unconstitutional, violates the separation of powers, and that warrantless trash searches violate a citizen's reasonable expectation of privacy under Article I, Section 8.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the district court's ruling, holding that Iowa Code section 808.16(3) is constitutional and that curbside garbage is abandoned property, allowing warrantless searches.

title: Rivas v. Brownell
description: Whether the supreme court possessed emergency powers to toll the statute of limitations during the COVID-19 pandemic, with the plaintiff arguing it did and the defendants arguing it did not.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that the supreme court possessed emergency powers to toll the statute of limitations during the pandemic and that the district court erred in ruling otherwise.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that the lawsuit was time-barred because the supreme court lacked the power to toll the statute of limitations, violating separation of powers and due process rights.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the district court's dismissal, holding that the supreme court's tolling provision was valid and the plaintiff's lawsuit was timely filed.

title: League of United Latin American Citizens of Iowa v. Pate
description: Whether the League of United Latin American Citizens of Iowa (LULAC) has standing to challenge a thirteen-year-old permanent injunction and seek an interpretation of the Iowa English Language Reaffirmation Act regarding non-English voting materials.
plaintiff_argument: LULAC argued it had organizational standing because the King injunction and the Secretary's interpretation of the Act impaired its voter mobilization efforts, diverted resources, and caused monetary costs, and that the Act's "rights exception" allowed non-English voting materials.
defendant_argument: The Secretary argued LULAC lacked standing because its alleged injuries were not legally cognizable and it was not a regulated party, and that the Act required all voting materials to be in English without the "rights exception" applying.
decision_outcome: The Iowa Supreme Court reversed the district court's ruling, concluding that LULAC lacked standing to bring the suit, and remanded the case for dismissal.

title: State v. Mumford
description: Whether the drug dog's sniff, including its nose briefly entering the vehicle's cabin during a lawful traffic stop, constituted an unconstitutional search under the Fourth Amendment and Article I, Section 8 of the Iowa Constitution, thereby requiring suppression of evidence, and whether there was sufficient evidence for the marijuana conviction.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the traffic stop was lawful due to an obscured license plate, the drug dog sniff, even with minimal intrusion into the vehicle's cabin, did not violate constitutional rights, and there was sufficient circumstantial evidence to support the marijuana conviction.
defendant_argument: Mumford argued that the traffic stop and the drug dog sniff, particularly the dog's nose entering the vehicle, constituted an unlawful search in violation of her federal and state constitutional rights, requiring suppression of evidence, and that there was insufficient evidence to prove the substance was marijuana.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed Mumford's convictions, finding no error in denying the motion to suppress evidence or in the sufficiency of evidence for possession of marijuana.

title: In re N.S.
description: Whether Iowa's statutory procedure for the restoration of firearm rights, lost due to an involuntary mental health commitment, survives a strict-scrutiny constitutional challenge under Amendment 1A, specifically regarding the burden of proof.
plaintiff_argument: N.S. argued that he met the statutory criteria for firearm rights restoration, and that Amendment 1A requires shifting the burden of proof to the State, making the current statute unconstitutional as applied to him because he is not currently dangerous.
defendant_argument: The State argued that the district court correctly applied the statutory criteria and rejected the constitutional challenge, asserting that Amendment 1A does not shift the burden of proof and that the statute is narrowly tailored to serve the compelling interest of preventing gun violence and suicide.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the district court's judgment denying N.S.'s petition for restoration of his firearm rights.

title: State v. Miller
description: Whether sentencing juvenile offenders to a minimum term of incarceration before parole eligibility without expert testimony or with an alleged improper presumption violates the Iowa Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the minimum sentence was constitutional, expert testimony was not required, and the district court properly applied sentencing factors without an improper presumption.
defendant_argument: Miller argued that minimum sentences for juveniles are unconstitutional, expert testimony is required, and the district court abused its discretion by presuming a minimum term and misapplying sentencing factors.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the district court's sentence of life imprisonment with the possibility of parole after 35 years for the juvenile offender.

title: State v. Bauler
description: Whether the United States or the Iowa Constitution was violated when a K-9 handler and his trained canine momentarily made contact with the exterior of a vehicle while performing an open-air dog sniff.
plaintiff_argument: The open-air dog sniff, involving physical contact by the dog and handler with her vehicle without a warrant, constituted an unconstitutional search under both the Fourth Amendment and the Iowa Constitution.
defendant_argument: The dog sniff was lawful because dog sniffs are "sui generis" and only reveal contraband, and momentary contact with the vehicle's exterior does not constitute an unconstitutional search or trespass.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the denial of Bauler's motion to suppress, upholding her convictions and sentence.

title: State v. White
description: Whether the use of a one-way closed-circuit television system for child witness testimony, where the defendant could see the witnesses but the witnesses could not see the defendant, violated the defendant's right to face-to-face confrontation under the Iowa Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the one-way video testimony procedure for child witnesses was permissible under Iowa Code and did not violate the defendant's constitutional confrontation rights, citing necessity to protect minors and existing precedent.
defendant_argument: White argued that the Iowa Constitution's confrontation clause requires face-to-face testimony with two-way visibility, and the one-way video system violated this right.
decision_outcome: The court reversed White's convictions and remanded for a new trial, holding that the one-way video testimony violated his confrontation rights under the Iowa Constitution.

title: Planned Parenthood of the Heartland, Inc, et al. v. Kim Reynolds, et al.
description: Whether a law prohibiting abortion after a fetal heartbeat is detected is constitutional under the Iowa Constitution, with the plaintiff arguing it is unconstitutional and the defendant arguing it is constitutional under rational basis review.
plaintiff_argument: The fetal heartbeat statute violates the due process clause, inalienable rights clause, and equal protection clause of the Iowa Constitution, and a temporary injunction should block its enforcement.
defendant_argument: The district court applied the wrong constitutional test; abortion is not a fundamental right under the Iowa Constitution, so the statute should be reviewed under the rational basis test and is constitutional.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the district court's order granting a temporary injunction, allowing the fetal heartbeat statute to take effect, and remanded the case for further proceedings.

title: Smith v. Iowa District Court for Polk County
description: Whether the Iowa Constitution supports a legislative privilege that protects Iowa legislators from compelled production of documents related to the passage of legislation, and if so, the scope of that privilege.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff legislators argued that they are protected from compelled document production by an absolute legislative privilege under the Iowa Constitution, stemming from principles of separation of powers and the right to make known opinions to representatives.
defendant_argument: The defendant (LULAC) argued that if a legislative privilege exists under Iowa law, it is qualified and should be abrogated in this case due to compelling constitutional rights at stake, making discovery into legislators' intent highly relevant to their claims of unconstitutional viewpoint discrimination.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the district court's judgment that granted LULAC's motion to compel, holding that the Iowa Constitution contains a legislative privilege that protects legislators from compelled document production, and remanded with instructions to quash the subpoenas.

title: Iowa Individual Health Benefit Reinsurance Association v. State University of Iowa
description: Whether state universities are required members of the Iowa Individual Health Benefit Reinsurance Association (IIHBRA) and subject to its assessments, and whether this statutory scheme violates the Iowa Constitution's prohibition against the state acting as a surety.
plaintiff_argument: The universities are statutorily required members of IIHBRA and must pay assessments, as they are 'persons' providing 'health benefit plans.' The statutory scheme creates a primary liability, not a suretyship, and thus does not violate the Iowa Constitution. IIHBRA is also authorized to impose late payment fees and should recover attorney fees.
defendant_argument: The universities are not members of IIHBRA because they do not fall within the specific enumerated subcategories of 'persons' providing health benefits subject to state insurance regulation. The statutory assessment scheme violates the Iowa Constitution by making the state a surety for others' debts. IIHBRA is not authorized to impose late payment fees or recover attorney fees.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed that the universities are members of IIHBRA and that the statutory scheme does not violate the Iowa Constitution. It reversed the district court's denial of late payment fees to IIHBRA but affirmed the denial of attorney fees and costs, remanding the case for entry of judgment including late payment fees.

title: Livingood v. City of Des Moines
description: Whether the City of Des Moines' use of the state's income offset program to collect automated traffic citation penalties, without first reducing them to a judgment, is lawful.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that the city's collection method for ATE penalties was an unlawful property tax, violated the statute of limitations, constituted an unconstitutional taking, was preempted by state law, violated due process, and amounted to unjust enrichment.
defendant_argument: The city contended that its ATE program administration was lawful, that the penalties were legally enforceable debts, and that its collection efforts were authorized by state law.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court affirmed in part and reversed in part the district court's judgment, remanding the case for further proceedings consistent with its opinion.

title: Valdez v. West Des Moines Community Schools
description: Whether the district court erred in overruling the plaintiff's Batson challenge to a peremptory juror strike and in granting a directed verdict for the defendant on individual liability for discrimination and wrongful discharge.
plaintiff_argument: Valdez argued the district court erred by overruling her Batson challenge to the peremptory strike of the only Black potential juror and by granting a directed verdict for Johnson, asserting Johnson should be individually liable for constructive discharge under the Iowa Civil Rights Act and common law.
defendant_argument: Defendants contended their peremptory strike of Juror 13 was race-neutral and that Johnson was not individually liable as she lacked supervisory authority to effectuate adverse employment actions or correct a hostile work environment.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the judgment of the district court, upholding its rulings on the Batson challenge, individual liability, and evidentiary matters.

title: Planned Parenthood of Heartland, Inc. v. Reynolds
description: Whether the permanent injunction against the enforcement of Iowa Code chapter 146C's 'fetal heartbeat' provision should be dissolved, thereby allowing the statute to take effect.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argues that the permanent injunction against the fetal heartbeat bill should remain in place because the bill is unconstitutional under the existing undue burden standard, which was not removed by previous court decisions.
defendant_argument: The defendant argues that the permanent injunction should be dissolved because there has been a substantial change in law (referencing Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Org.), and the fetal heartbeat bill is constitutional under a rational basis review.
decision_outcome: The Iowa Supreme Court, being evenly divided, affirmed the district court's denial of the State's motion to dissolve the permanent injunction, meaning the injunction against the 'fetal heartbeat' bill remains in effect by operation of law.

title: State ex rel. Attorney General of Iowa v. Autor
description: Whether the Iowa Consumer Fraud Act's (CFA) requirement for civil enforcement actions to be by equitable proceedings violates the constitutional right to a jury trial.
plaintiff_argument: The Attorney General argued that the CFA's requirement for civil actions to be by equitable proceedings means defendants are not entitled to a jury trial, as equitable actions traditionally do not involve juries.
defendant_argument: The defendants contended that the constitutional right to a jury trial applies because the Attorney General was seeking substantial monetary remedies, such as disgorgement and civil penalties, which they argued are legal remedies.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the district court's decision to strike the defendants' jury demand and remanded the case for further proceedings.

title: Burnett v. Smith
description: Whether a constitutional tort claim for damages can be pursued under Article I, Section 8 of the Iowa Constitution, and whether the precedent set in Godfrey v. State should be overruled.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that his passive noncooperation did not provide probable cause for arrest, and his constitutional rights under Article I, Section 8 of the Iowa Constitution were violated by an unlawful arrest, seeking to uphold the precedent of Godfrey v. State for a constitutional tort claim.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that Godfrey v. State was wrongly decided and should be overruled, asserting that Officer Smith exercised due care and was entitled to immunity, and that Article I, Section 8 does not provide a self-executing constitutional tort claim for damages.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the district court's judgment, overruling the precedent set in Godfrey v. State, and no longer recognizing a standalone cause of action for money damages under the Iowa Constitution unless authorized by common law, statute, or express constitutional terms.

title: State v. Abu Youm
description: Whether the emergency aid doctrine, a branch of the community caretaking exception, justified the warrantless entry into Sam Daniel Abu Youm's apartment, with the plaintiff arguing it was justified due to exigent circumstances and the defendant arguing it was an unlawful search violating Fourth Amendment rights.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the warrantless entry was justified under the emergency aid doctrine due to reports of gunshots, a man lying on the balcony, and suspicious behavior, which constituted exigent circumstances.
defendant_argument: Abu Youm argued that the warrantless entry violated his Fourth Amendment rights because no true emergency existed, and the officers' actions did not demonstrate the urgency required for the emergency aid doctrine to apply.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the decision of the court of appeals and the district court judgment, upholding Abu Youm's convictions and denying his motion to suppress.

title: LS Power Midcontinent, LLC v. State
description: Whether Iowa legislation granting incumbent electric transmission owners a right of first refusal for new projects is constitutional under the single-subject, title, and equal protection clauses, and whether non-incumbent competitors have standing to challenge it.
plaintiff_argument: LSP argues they have standing because the ROFR directly injures them by precluding competitive bidding, and the legislation is unconstitutional due to violations of the single-subject, title, and equal protection clauses of the Iowa Constitution.
defendant_argument: The State and intervenors argue LSP lacks standing because no specific project was lost, and the ROFR legislation is constitutional.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the lower courts' dismissal for lack of standing, found LSP likely to succeed on the merits of its constitutional challenge, and granted a temporary injunction to stay enforcement of the ROFR, remanding the case for a decision on the merits.

title: State v. Sallis
description: Whether an officer's several-months-old recollection of a motorist's barred driving status constitutes reasonable suspicion for a traffic stop, and whether a criminal defendant with appointed counsel has a constitutional right to have a retained attorney enter a limited appearance.
plaintiff_argument: The traffic stop was invalid because the officer's information about his barred driving status was stale, and the district court violated his Sixth Amendment right to counsel by denying his retained attorney's requests for limited appearances.
defendant_argument: The traffic stop was justified by reasonable suspicion based on the officer's prior knowledge of Sallis's barred driving status, and the district court properly regulated legal appearances, as there is no unlimited constitutional right to limited appearances in cases with appointed counsel.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed Sallis's conviction and sentence, upholding the denial of his motion to suppress and the denial of his retained attorney's requests for limited appearances.

title: Planned Parenthood of the Heartland, Inc. v. Reynolds ex rel. State
description: Whether the Iowa Constitution provides a fundamental right to an abortion, requiring strict scrutiny for regulations, and whether a 24-hour waiting period for abortion violates the single-subject rule or is barred by issue preclusion.
plaintiff_argument: Planned Parenthood argued that the 24-hour waiting period violated the single-subject rule and that the prior decision in PPH II had issue preclusive effect, barring the State from relitigating the issue. They also argued that the Iowa Constitution protects a fundamental right to abortion, requiring strict scrutiny.
defendant_argument: The State argued that the 24-hour waiting period did not violate the single-subject rule, that issue preclusion did not apply, and that the court should overrule PPH II, which had established a fundamental right to abortion under the Iowa Constitution.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the district court's grant of summary judgment to Planned Parenthood, concluding that the 2020 legislation did not violate the single-subject rule and that issue preclusion did not bar the State from seeking to overrule PPH II. The court explicitly overruled PPH II, holding that the Iowa Constitution is not the source of a fundamental right to an abortion requiring strict scrutiny, and remanded the case for further proceedings.

title: Landowners v. South Central Regional Airport Agency
description: Whether the 28E Agreement, which created the South Central Regional Airport Agency (SCRAA), is constitutionally valid given that it binds future county boards of supervisors in their legislative functions and restricts the County's ability to unilaterally withdraw from the agreement.
plaintiff_argument: The Landowners and Mahaska County argued that the 28E Agreement is unconstitutional because it binds future boards of supervisors indefinitely and prevents the County from terminating its participation in the same manner it commenced, thereby unlawfully restricting its legislative powers.
defendant_argument: The Cities of Pella and Oskaloosa argued that the 28E Agreement is valid and enforceable, allowing for the delegation of governmental functions and unlimited duration, and that the County cannot unilaterally withdraw.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court of Iowa reversed the district court's grant of summary judgment in favor of the Cities, finding the 28E Agreement constitutionally infirm because it unlawfully binds future boards of supervisors and restricts the County's ability to terminate its delegation of powers. Article XI of the Agreement was declared invalid and severed, allowing Mahaska County to withdraw by a valid vote of its board of supervisors.

title: State v. Price-Williams
description: Whether law enforcement violated Price-Williams's Fourth Amendment and state constitutional rights against unreasonable search and seizure by ordering him out of a vehicle and patting him down without reasonable suspicion, and whether his admission to possessing a firearm should be suppressed due to a lack of Miranda warning.
plaintiff_argument: Price-Williams argued that law enforcement violated his rights under Article I, Section 8 of the Iowa Constitution and the Fourth Amendment by ordering him out of the vehicle and patting him down without reasonable and articulable facts, and that his admission to possessing a firearm should be suppressed due to questioning without a Miranda warning.
defendant_argument: The State argued that the officer had reasonable suspicion to justify ordering Price-Williams out of the vehicle and patting him down for weapons, and that the Miranda claim was not separately relied upon as reasonable suspicion existed regardless of the admission.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the court of appeals decision and district court judgment, denying Price-Williams's motion to suppress and upholding his conviction for being a felon in possession of a firearm.

title: State v. Hauge
description: Whether law enforcement acted unreasonably under the Fourth Amendment and Iowa Constitution by ordering a passenger out of a vehicle and conducting a pat-down search, and whether the passenger's consent to the pat-down was voluntary.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the officer's order for Hauge to exit the vehicle was necessary to facilitate a lawful arrest of another passenger, and that Hauge's consent to the pat-down was voluntary without requiring an advisement of the right to refuse.
defendant_argument: Hauge argued that law enforcement lacked justification to order him out of the vehicle and that his consent to the pat-down was not voluntary because he was not informed of his right to decline the search.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the district court's judgment, ruling that the officer's order for the passenger to exit the vehicle was necessary for a lawful arrest and that the passenger's consent to the pat-down was voluntary.

title: State v. Basquin
description: Whether the Iowa Supreme Court's COVID-19 supervisory orders, which allowed written felony guilty pleas in lieu of in-person colloquies, violated due process and separation of powers, as argued by the defendant, or if the court had the constitutional and inherent authority to issue such orders without violating these principles, as argued by the State.
plaintiff_argument: Basquin argued that the court's supervisory orders allowing written felony guilty pleas violated rules of criminal procedure, precedent, due process, and separation of powers, requiring an in-person plea colloquy.
defendant_argument: The State argued that the court had constitutional and inherent authority to permit written guilty pleas to felonies during the pandemic, and that its supervisory orders did not violate due process or separation of powers.
decision_outcome: The court upheld its supervisory orders as lawful exercises of its constitutional and inherent authority during the pandemic, rejecting Basquin's due process and separation of powers challenges, and affirmed his conviction.

title: State v. Lilly
description: Whether Kenneth Lilly's right to an impartial jury was violated due to the systematic exclusion of African-Americans from jury pools, with Lilly asserting a violation and the State denying it.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that Lilly failed to prove systematic exclusion or that the challenged jury selection practices caused underrepresentation, and that the practices were 'run-of-the-mill' and permissible.
defendant_argument: Lilly argued that the jury selection process, using voter registration and ID lists, systematically excluded African-Americans because low-income individuals (a higher percentage of whom are African-American) register at lower rates.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the district court's ruling that Kenneth Lilly failed to prove a violation of his right to an impartial jury, thereby upholding his conviction.

title: State v. Wright
description: Whether a peace officer, without a warrant, can take a citizen's opaque trash bags left outside for collection, open them, and rummage through their contents for criminal investigation.
plaintiff_argument: The officer's warrantless search of his trash bags violated his constitutional rights under federal and state law, as it involved physical trespass and an invasion of his reasonable expectation of privacy, especially given local anti-scavenging ordinances.
defendant_argument: Wright abandoned his trash, thus he had no reasonable expectation of privacy in it, and the officer's conduct was justified for law enforcement purposes.
decision_outcome: The court ruled that the warrantless search and seizure of Wright's trash bags violated Article I, Section 8 of the Iowa Constitution, and remanded the case for the suppression of evidence obtained from these searches.

title: Godfrey v. State
description: Whether Christopher J. Godfrey, a state-appointed officer, was subjected to sexual-orientation discrimination and retaliation under the Iowa Civil Rights Act (ICRA) and whether his constitutional right to a particular salary was violated.
plaintiff_argument: Godfrey argued he was discriminated against and retaliated against due to his sexual orientation, and that his constitutional right to a specific salary level was violated when his pay was reduced.
defendant_argument: The State argued that ICRA did not apply to Godfrey as an appointed officer, there was no evidence Governor Branstad knew Godfrey was gay, Godfrey's actions were not protected activity for retaliation, and he had no constitutionally protected property interest in his salary.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the judgment of the district court and remanded the case for dismissal of all of the plaintiff's claims.

title: Planned Parenthood of the Heartland, Inc. v. Reynolds
description: Whether Iowa's law, which prohibits abortion providers from receiving federal grants for sex education programs, violates constitutional rights, including equal protection, free speech, free association, and due process.
plaintiff_argument: Planned Parenthood of the Heartland (PPH) argues the Act violates its equal protection rights by unconstitutionally distinguishing between those who provide and advocate for abortion and those who do not, and that it conditions the receipt of government funds on PPH giving up its rights to free speech, free association, and a due process right to provide abortions.
defendant_argument: The State argues the funding conditions are rationally related to the classification selected by the general assembly, as an abortion provider lacks a freestanding constitutional right to provide abortions, and the state has a legitimate interest in selecting the messenger for its programs and expressing a preference for childbirth.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the district court's order, concluding that the Act's funding conditions are constitutional and do not violate PPH's equal protection rights or the unconstitutional conditions doctrine.

title: Iowa Citizens for Community Improvement v. State
description: Whether the State of Iowa has an affirmative duty under the public trust doctrine to protect navigable waters from agricultural nonpoint source pollution, and whether the plaintiffs have standing to compel the State to enact mandatory pollution controls.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argue that the State of Iowa violated the public trust doctrine by failing to protect the Raccoon River from agricultural pollution, leading to increased water treatment costs and impaired recreational use, and seek a mandatory remedial plan.
defendant_argument: The defendants argue that the plaintiffs lack standing because their alleged injuries are speculative and not redressable by the court, and the issue is a nonjusticiable political question that should be resolved by the legislative branch.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the district court's order, concluding that the plaintiffs lacked standing and the issue was a nonjusticiable political question, and remanded with instructions to dismiss the petition.

title: State v. Sewell
description: Whether Iowa law or the Iowa Constitution guarantee a suspected drunk driver the right to a private phone consultation with counsel before deciding whether to take a blood alcohol test.
plaintiff_argument: Sewell argued that Iowa Code section 804.20 and the Iowa Constitution (Article I, Sections 9 and 10) provide a right to a private phone consultation with counsel before deciding on a blood alcohol test.
defendant_argument: The State argued that Iowa Code section 804.20 does not provide a right to a private phone consultation, as calls must be made in the presence of the custodian, and that the Iowa Constitution's right to counsel only attaches in formal criminal prosecutions, not pre-prosecution chemical testing decisions.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed Sewell's conviction and sentence, concluding he was not entitled to a private phone consultation with counsel under Iowa law or the Iowa Constitution.

title: State v. Treptow
description: Whether Iowa Code sections 814.6 and 814.7, which limit direct appeals for guilty pleas and mandate postconviction relief for ineffective assistance of counsel claims, violate the separation of powers, equal protection, and due process doctrines, and whether the defendant has established good cause to pursue a direct appeal.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that Iowa Code sections 814.6 and 814.7 are constitutional, do not violate separation of powers, equal protection, or due process, and that Treptow failed to establish good cause for a direct appeal.
defendant_argument: Treptow argued that Iowa Code sections 814.6 and 814.7 violate separation of powers, equal protection, and due process, and that he had good cause to appeal, especially regarding the factual basis of his guilty plea.
decision_outcome: The court dismissed Treptow's appeal, ruling that he failed to establish good cause for a direct appeal and upholding the constitutionality of Iowa Code sections 814.6 and 814.7.

title: Hrbek v. State
description: Whether Iowa Code § 822.3A, which prohibits represented postconviction-relief applicants from filing pro se supplemental documents, is applicable retrospectively and constitutional, with the plaintiff arguing it is inapplicable and unconstitutional, and the defendant arguing it is applicable and constitutional.
plaintiff_argument: Hrbek contends the new law is inapplicable retrospectively to pending cases and is unconstitutional, violating the separation-of-powers doctrine and his right to file pro se supplemental documents.
defendant_argument: The State argues the new law applies prospectively to future filings, is constitutional, and does not violate the separation-of-powers doctrine or any constitutional right to hybrid representation.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the district court's order prohibiting Hrbek from filing additional pro se supplemental documents and directed the clerk to strike Hrbek's pro se supplemental briefs, ruling that Iowa Code § 822.3A is applicable and constitutional.

title: State ex rel. Dickey v. Besler
description: Whether the Governor's appointment of a district court judge was timely made according to constitutional and statutory deadlines, and whether a citizen has standing to challenge this appointment via a quo warranto action, making the issue justiciable.
plaintiff_argument: Dickey argued that the Governor failed to appoint Judge Besler within the thirty-day deadline, rendering his holding of office unlawful, and that he, as a citizen, attorney, and taxpayer, had standing to challenge this through a quo warranto action, which he believed was a justiciable legal question.
defendant_argument: Besler argued that the Governor did make the appointment within the thirty-day period by communicating her decision to her chief of staff, that Dickey lacked standing, and that the Chief Justice's acceptance of the appointment as timely made the issue a nonjusticiable political question, precluding judicial review.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the district court's judgment, concluding that the case presented a nonjusticiable controversy because both the Governor and the Chief Justice had accepted the appointment as timely.

title: State v. Thompson
description: Whether the district court erred in admitting evidence of Thompson's residential address and whether Iowa Code section 814.6A, which prohibits represented defendants from filing pro se documents, violates the separation of powers doctrine.
plaintiff_argument: Thompson argued that the residential address evidence was irrelevant and unfairly prejudicial, and that Iowa Code section 814.6A violates the separation of powers doctrine by impeding the appellate courts' essential functioning and a defendant's right to present legal claims.
defendant_argument: The State argued that the residential address evidence was relevant to prove Thompson's knowledge and intent, and that Iowa Code section 814.6A is a proper exercise of the legislature's constitutional authority to regulate court practice and procedure.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed Thompson's convictions for attempting to obtain a prescription drug by deceit and rejected his constitutional challenge to Iowa Code section 814.6A, denying his motion to accept a pro se supplemental brief.
